title: AVD Monitoring and Insights: Log Analytics, Workbooks, and KQL
summary: Before you can operate an Azure Virtual Desktop estate at scale you need eyes on it, and that starts with Azure Virtual Desktop Insights. This lesson walks through the full monitoring data path: enabling diagnostic settings on host pools and workspaces, wiring session hosts to a Log Analytics workspace through the Azure Monitor Agent and a data collection rule, and understanding the family of WVD-prefixed tables that carry connection, error, checkpoint, host-registration, agent-health, and network telemetry. You'll write real KQL queries against verified table and column names to find connection failures, track round-trip time, and calculate session duration, then set up log alerts so problems surface before users complain.
objectives: Explain what Azure Virtual Desktop Insights is built on and what data sources feed it
Enable AVD diagnostic settings on host pools and workspaces and identify the supported diagnostic categories
Configure the Azure Monitor Agent data collection path for session hosts using a data collection rule
Identify the core WVD Log Analytics tables and the columns each one actually contains
Write KQL queries to find connection failures, round-trip time trends, and per-user session duration
Configure an Azure Monitor log alert against AVD telemetry

quiz.q: Azure Virtual Desktop Insights is a dashboard built on top of which Azure Monitor feature?
options: A standalone Log Analytics workspace with no other dependency
quiz.why: Microsoft Learn describes Azure Virtual Desktop Insights as 'a dashboard built on Azure Monitor Workbooks.' It reads from a Log Analytics workspace, but the dashboard layer itself is Workbooks.

quiz.q: Which agent does Microsoft require today to collect performance counters and Windows Event Logs from AVD session hosts for Insights?
options: The Azure Monitor Agent (AMA), associated to hosts via a Data Collection Rule
No agent is needed; diagnostic settings cover everything
quiz.why: Current AVD Insights setup requires the Azure Monitor Agent plus a Data Collection Rule on each session host. The legacy Log Analytics (MMA) agent was deprecated August 31, 2024, and its backend services stop entirely on March 2, 2026 — do not design new monitoring on it.

quiz.q: Which table would you query to see the estimated round-trip time for a user's connection?
quiz.why: WVDConnectionNetworkData carries EstRoundTripTimeInMs and EstAvailableBandwidthKBps, keyed by CorrelationId and TimeGenerated. WVDConnections has connection metadata and state, not network quality metrics.

quiz.q: In the WVDErrors table, which column tells you whether an error is a Microsoft service-side problem you must escalate, versus one you can likely resolve yourself?
quiz.why: ServiceError is a boolean. When it's true, escalate to Microsoft support and supply the CorrelationId. When it's false, the error is something an admin task can typically resolve.

quiz.q: Which host pool diagnostic category and table pair correctly reports whether the AVD agent on a session host is currently healthy?
quiz.why: The AgentHealthStatus diagnostic category writes to the WVDAgentHealthStatus table, which includes Status, LastHeartBeat, ActiveSessions, and AgentVersion per session host.

quiz.q: You want the average session duration for users over the last day, using the WVDConnections table you already have enabled. Describe, in your own words, the approach you'd take in KQL to compute it (exact syntax not required).
quiz.answer: Filter WVDConnections to the last day, then use CorrelationId as the join key that ties together the rows for a single connection: the row where State == "Connected" gives the start time (its TimeGenerated), and the row where State == "Completed" for the same CorrelationId gives the end time. Join those two projections on CorrelationId, compute the time difference between the two TimeGenerated values as the session duration, and then summarize (e.g., average) that duration, optionally grouped by UserName or SessionHostName.
quiz.why: This mirrors the documented connection state machine (Started, Connected, Completed) and the CorrelationId-based self-join Microsoft's own sample query uses to compute session duration.

body_markdown:
## Why Monitoring Gets Its Own AZ-140 Domain

Everything you built in Modules 3 through 5 — host pools, networking, golden images, identity, FSLogix — eventually meets real users on a Tuesday morning, and something will go sideways. AZ-140's fourth domain, Monitor and maintain AVD infrastructure, exists because a platform you can't observe is a platform you can only guess about. This lesson builds the observability foundation the rest of Module 6 assumes: Azure Virtual Desktop Insights, the Log Analytics tables underneath it, and the KQL you'll actually run at 8am when the help desk queue starts filling up.

## What Azure Virtual Desktop Insights Actually Is

AVD Insights is not a separate monitoring product. It's a dashboard built on **Azure Monitor Workbooks**, reading data out of a Log Analytics workspace that you point at your AVD environment. Open it at `aka.ms/avdi` in the Azure portal, and the first thing you should do on a new environment is run its **Check Configuration** workbook — it audits whether the pieces below are actually wired up, and gives you one-click remediation when they aren't.

Two RBAC roles are the minimum to view it: **Desktop Virtualization Reader** on the resource group/subscription holding your host pools, and **Log Analytics Reader** on the workspace. Neither role lets you *change* anything — that still requires separate AVD admin permissions.

## The Data Path: Diagnostic Settings + Azure Monitor Agent

Insights needs two independent data feeds, and it's a common deployment mistake to set up only one:

1. **Resource diagnostic settings** on the AVD host pool and workspace objects (these are Azure Resource Manager objects, not VMs). You enable the diagnostic categories: **Management Activities, Feed, Connections, Errors, Checkpoints, HostRegistration, AgentHealthStatus** (host pool) and **Management Activities, Feed, Errors, Checkpoints** (workspace), each streamed to your designated Log Analytics workspace.
2. **Session host telemetry** via the **Azure Monitor Agent (AMA)**, associated to each session host through a **Data Collection Rule (DCR)** that defines which performance counters and Windows Event Logs to collect. This is a per-VM agent install, not a resource-level setting, and it's the part people forget after adding new hosts to a pool.

A critical, exam-relevant fact: the legacy **Log Analytics agent (MMA)** is not an option here. Microsoft deprecated it on **August 31, 2024**, data uploads were scheduled to briefly pause on **January 26, 2026** as a test, and the backend services shut down entirely on **March 2, 2026**. If you inherit an environment still running MMA for AVD monitoring, migrating it to AMA is not optional maintenance — it's a hard deadline that has now passed the point of safe delay.

## The WVD Table Family

Every AVD-related table in Log Analytics is prefixed `WVD` (a holdover from the service's original Windows Virtual Desktop name). The ones you'll use constantly:

| Table | What it holds | Key columns |
|---|---|---|
| `WVDConnections` | Connection lifecycle events (Started/Connected/Completed) | `CorrelationId`, `UserName`, `State`, `SessionHostName`, `ResourceAlias`, `TransportType`, `TimeGenerated` |
| `WVDErrors` | Errors across management, host registration, and feed activity | `CodeSymbolic`, `Code`, `Message`, `ServiceError`, `Source`, `CorrelationId`, `UserName` |
| `WVDCheckpoints` | Intermediate steps within an activity (e.g., app launches inside a desktop session) | `ActivityType`, `Name`, `CorrelationId`, `Parameters` |
| `WVDHostRegistrations` | Whether a session host successfully registered with the service | `SessionHostName`, `SessionHostIPAddress`, `CorrelationId` |
| `WVDAgentHealthStatus` | Live health/heartbeat of the AVD agent per host, roughly every 30 seconds | `SessionHostName`, `Status`, `AgentVersion`, `ActiveSessions`, `InactiveSessions`, `LastHeartBeat` |
| `WVDConnectionNetworkData` | Estimated network quality per connection | `CorrelationId`, `EstRoundTripTimeInMs`, `EstAvailableBandwidthKBps` |
| `WVDManagement` | Admin/API/PowerShell management activity | `CorrelationId`, `ActivityType` |
| `WVDFeeds` | Whether users could subscribe to a workspace's app feed | `CorrelationId`, `UserName` |

Note the exact casing and pluralization — `WVDHostRegistrations` and `WVDFeeds` are plural, `WVDManagement` is not `WVDManagementActivities`, and there is no `WVDErrors` alternate spelling. Typos here are the single most common reason a working query returns zero rows.

## Starter KQL Queries You'll Actually Run

**Connection failures in the last 24 hours, grouped by cause:**

```kusto
WVDErrors
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ServiceError == false
| summarize FailureCount = count() by CodeSymbolic, Source
| sort by FailureCount desc
```

Filtering `ServiceError == false` isolates admin-actionable errors first; flip it to `true` to see what you'd need to open a Microsoft support case for.

**Round-trip time trend over the last week:**

```kusto
WVDConnectionNetworkData
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| summarize AvgRoundTripMs = avg(EstRoundTripTimeInMs), AvgBandwidthKBps = avg(EstAvailableBandwidthKBps) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| render timechart
```

**Session duration by user, using the documented CorrelationId self-join pattern:**

```kusto
let Events = WVDConnections | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d);
Events
| where State == "Connected"
| project CorrelationId, UserName, SessionHostName, StartTime = TimeGenerated
| join kind=inner (
    Events
    | where State == "Completed"
    | project CorrelationId, EndTime = TimeGenerated
) on CorrelationId
| extend DurationMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', EndTime, StartTime)
| project UserName, SessionHostName, DurationMinutes
| sort by DurationMinutes desc
```

**Session hosts currently reporting unhealthy:**

```kusto
WVDAgentHealthStatus
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by SessionHostName
| where Status != "Healthy"
| project SessionHostName, Status, AgentVersion, LastHeartBeat
```

`arg_max` here picks the most recent heartbeat row per host so you're not double-counting stale status snapshots.

## Alerting on What Matters

Dashboards you have to remember to open don't catch 2am problems. Wrap the queries above (or simpler thresholds) in **Azure Monitor log alerts**: an alert rule on a scheduled query, with an action group that pages your on-call or posts to a Teams channel. Reasonable first alerts for a production estate: a spike in `WVDErrors` with `ServiceError == false` over a short window (config/auth problems), any `WVDAgentHealthStatus` row reporting `Status != "Healthy"` for more than a few minutes, and a sustained rise in average `EstRoundTripTimeInMs`. Start with a small set of high-signal alerts — alert fatigue from noisy thresholds is what gets monitoring ignored six weeks after go-live.

## What You'd Actually Do

On a new AVD environment: create a dedicated Log Analytics workspace for AVD, run the Insights Check Configuration workbook, enable diagnostic settings on every host pool and workspace, deploy AMA plus a DCR to every session host (Azure Policy can auto-remediate this as hosts are added), confirm data is flowing with a quick `WVDConnections | take 10`, then build two or three log alerts before you call monitoring 'done.' Everything in the rest of this module — image lifecycle, troubleshooting, day-2 operations — assumes this pipeline is already live.

slides.title: Two Independent Data Feeds
bullets: Resource diagnostic settings on host pool and workspace objects
Categories: Management Activities, Feed, Connections, Errors, Checkpoints, HostRegistration, AgentHealthStatus
Session host telemetry needs the Azure Monitor Agent
AMA is associated per VM through a Data Collection Rule
Forgetting the DCR on new hosts is the most common gap
slides.narration: Insights depends on two feeds that are easy to set up only one of. First, resource diagnostic settings on the host pool and workspace objects themselves, covering categories like management activities, feed, connections, errors, checkpoints, host registration, and agent health status. Second, session host telemetry, which requires installing the Azure Monitor Agent on every session host and associating it with a data collection rule. That second piece is per virtual machine, not per resource, and it's exactly what people forget when they add new hosts to an existing pool.

New AVD monitoring must be built on the Azure Monitor Agent
If you inherit MMA-based monitoring, migration is not optional
slides.narration: One fact you cannot get wrong on the exam or in production: the legacy Log Analytics agent, sometimes called the MMA agent, is not a valid choice for new monitoring. It was deprecated in August 2024, its data upload path was paused briefly in January 2026 as a shutdown warning, and its backend services stopped completely on March 2nd, 2026. If you walk into an environment still using it, treat migrating to the Azure Monitor Agent as urgent infrastructure work, not routine maintenance.

slides.title: The WVD Table Family
bullets: Every AVD table in Log Analytics is prefixed WVD
WVDConnections: connection lifecycle and state
WVDErrors: failures, with a ServiceError flag
WVDAgentHealthStatus: per-host heartbeat and status
WVDConnectionNetworkData: round trip time and bandwidth
slides.narration: Every table related to Azure Virtual Desktop carries the W V D prefix, a holdover from the service's original name. The ones you'll use constantly are WVDConnections for connection lifecycle and state, WVDErrors for failures with a ServiceError flag telling you whether to escalate to Microsoft, WVDAgentHealthStatus for per host heartbeat and status roughly every thirty seconds, and WVDConnectionNetworkData for round trip time and estimated bandwidth per connection.

slides.title: Get the Table Names Exactly Right
bullets: WVDHostRegistrations and WVDFeeds are plural
WVDManagement, not WVDManagementActivities
WVDCheckpoints tracks steps inside an activity
WVDConnections has State values Started, Connected, Completed
A typo here is the top reason a query returns zero rows
slides.narration: Casing and pluralization matter more than you'd expect. It's WVDHostRegistrations and WVDFeeds, both plural, and WVDManagement, not WVDManagementActivities. WVDCheckpoints tracks the specific steps reached inside an activity, like which app a user opened. And WVDConnections uses a small state machine with values Started, Connected, and Completed, which is exactly what lets you calculate session duration. Get any of these names slightly wrong and your query will run successfully and just return nothing, which is worse than an error.

slides.title: Query: Connection Failures
bullets: Filter WVDErrors to a recent time window
Split on ServiceError true versus false
False means it's likely admin-actionable
True means escalate to Microsoft with the CorrelationId
Group by CodeSymbolic to find your top failure causes
slides.narration: Your first go to query is against WVDErrors. Filter to the last day, then split on the ServiceError column. When it's false, the issue is something you can likely resolve yourself, a configuration or permissions problem. When it's true, it's a service side issue and you escalate to Microsoft support, always including the CorrelationId so they can trace the exact event. Grouping by CodeSymbolic quickly surfaces your top recurring failure causes.

slides.title: Query: Round Trip Time and Session Duration
bullets: WVDConnectionNetworkData holds EstRoundTripTimeInMs
Trend it hourly with render timechart
Session duration needs a self-join on CorrelationId
Connected row is the start, Completed row is the end
datetime_diff gives you the duration in minutes
slides.narration: For network quality, WVDConnectionNetworkData holds an estimated round trip time in milliseconds and estimated available bandwidth. Bin that hourly and render it as a time chart to spot degradation trends. For session duration, there's no single column for it. You join WVDConnections to itself on CorrelationId, treating the Connected state row as the start time and the Completed state row as the end time for that same connection, then take the difference between the two timestamps.

slides.title: Alert Before Users Complain
bullets: Wrap key queries in Azure Monitor log alert rules
Route alerts to an action group: email, Teams, on-call
Start with a small set of high signal alerts
Watch WVDErrors spikes, unhealthy agent status, rising RTT
Alert fatigue from noisy thresholds gets monitoring ignored
slides.narration: A dashboard you have to remember to open won't catch a two AM problem. Wrap your highest value queries in Azure Monitor log alert rules, routed to an action group that emails, posts to Teams, or pages your on call engineer. Start small: a spike in admin actionable WVDErrors, any session host reporting unhealthy agent status for more than a few minutes, and a sustained rise in round trip time are enough to start. Too many noisy alerts is how monitoring gets ignored a few weeks after go live.

slides.title: What You'd Actually Do
bullets: Create a dedicated Log Analytics workspace for AVD
Run Check Configuration, fix every gap it flags
Deploy AMA plus a DCR to every session host via Azure Policy
Confirm data flow with a simple WVDConnections query
Build two or three alerts before calling monitoring done
slides.narration: On a brand new AVD environment, here's the sequence. Create a dedicated Log Analytics workspace for AVD data. Run the Check Configuration workbook and fix every gap it flags. Deploy the Azure Monitor Agent and a data collection rule to every session host, ideally enforced automatically through Azure Policy as new hosts join. Confirm data is actually flowing with a simple query against WVDConnections. Then build two or three log alerts before you consider monitoring finished. Everything else in this module, image lifecycle, troubleshooting, day two operations, assumes this pipeline is already live.
